\textbf{Yes.} $\vec v$ and $\vec w$ are independent (not multiples of each other). Add $\vec e_3$ and $\vec e_4$:
\[\det\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0&0\\3&0&0&0\\2&2&1&0\\0&2&0&1\end{bmatrix}=-3\ne0,\]
so $\{\vec v,\vec w,\vec e_3,\vec e_4\}$ is linearly independent, and four independent vectors in $\mathbb R^4$ form a basis.
3:
$\det B=2(4-1)-1(2-1)+1(1-2)=4\ne0$, so $B$ is invertible. Row reducing $[B\mid I]$ (or using the adjugate):
\[B^{-1}=\boxed{\frac14\begin{pmatrix}3&-1&-1\\-1&3&-1\\-1&-1&3\end{pmatrix}}.\]
4:
Expand repeatedly along columns with a single nonzero entry. Column 1 gives $-1$; then the $(2,2)$ entry gives $-41$; then the row of the remaining $3\times3$ block $\begin{pmatrix}3&1&6\\0&2&0\\2&2&-1\end{pmatrix}$ with a single entry gives $2$; what's left is $\begin{pmatrix}3&6\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$ with $\lambda^2-2\lambda-15=(\lambda-5)(\lambda+3)$.
\[\boxed{\lambda=-1,\ -41,\ 2,\ 5,\ -3}.\]
5:
$S=\text{null}(D^T)$: $x_1+3x_2=0$ and $x_1+3x_3+6x_4=0$. With $x_3,x_4$ free, $x_1=-3x_3-6x_4$, $x_2=x_3+2x_4$:
\[S=\text{span}\{(-3,1,1,0),\ (-6,2,0,1)\}\quad(\text{both dot to }0\text{ with each column}).\]
7:
The matrix of $T$ (in the order $w,x,y,z$) is
\[\begin{bmatrix}5&-1&0&0\\2&0&0&0\\7&2&1&0\\13&41&11&4\end{bmatrix},\quad \det=8\ne0.\]
It is invertible, so $\ker T=\{\vec0\}$ and \boxed{\dim\ker T=0}. (Directly: $2w=0\Rightarrow w=0$, then $x=0$, $y=0$, $z=0$.)
8:
$G=ABA^{-1}$ is similar to $B$: same eigenvalues \boxed{2\ (\text{twice}),\ -1}. If $B\vec u=\lambda\vec u$ then $G(A\vec u)=AB\vec u=\lambda A\vec u$, so the eigenvectors of $G$ are $A$ times those of $B$ (the columns of $A$):
\[E_2=\text{span}\{(1,2,-1),\ (0,1,3)\},\qquad E_{-1}=\text{span}\{(0,0,1)\}.\]
10:
$AB=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. So $T$ is a horizontal shear $(x,y)\mapsto(x-y,y)$ followed by a rotation by $180^\circ$ (point reflection through the origin). The face is turned upside down and slanted: points with $y>0$ are pushed left before the rotation, so the image's top half leans right, and the eyes end up below the center with the smile on top. The origin stays fixed and $(1,0)\mapsto(-1,0)$.

\textbf{Bonus.} $\det A(x)=x^3-3x+2=(x-1)^2(x+2)$, so $A(x)$ is invertible for \boxed{x\ne1,\ -2}. Writing $A(x)=(x-1)I+J$ with $J$ the all-ones matrix ($J^2=3J$):
\[A(x)^{-1}=\boxed{\frac{1}{x-1}\Big(I-\frac{1}{x+2}J\Big)}.\]
